opus-5.5.text:
I think what's most remarkable about Terry is the sheer breadth. Most great mathematicians go very deep in one area and spend their whole career there. Terry has made fundamental contributions across harmonic analysis, PDEs, combinatorics, number theory, random matrix theory, compressed sensing. He moves between fields that most people would consider completely separate disciplines, and he's world-class in each one.

But beyond the breadth, what strikes me is how open he is. He blogs, he explains his thinking in public, he shares half-finished ideas, and he runs collaborative projects where anyone can contribute. A lot of mathematicians are protective of their work until it's polished. Terry seems to genuinely believe mathematics moves faster when it's done in the open, and he acts on that.

And that connects to what we care about at Harmonic. Terry has been very forward-looking about tools: formal verification, proof assistants like Lean, and AI. He isn't dismissive and he isn't hyping it either. He's experimenting, figuring out where these tools actually help today, and thinking carefully about how they might change the way mathematics gets done. When someone at his level takes that seriously and engages with it so thoughtfully, it shifts the whole community's perspective. That combination of brilliance, generosity, and curiosity about new ways of working is pretty rare.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts mathematicians who go deep in one area with Tao’s fundamental contributions across many fields, saying he is world-class in each. This conveys depth across domains as the remarkable breadth.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most about Terry is the breadth. Most mathematicians, even extraordinary ones, go deep in one area and spend their careers there. Terry moves across harmonic analysis, number theory, PDEs, combinatorics, random matrix theory, and he's not just visiting those fields, he's producing results that people in each of them consider foundational. The Green-Tao theorem on arithmetic progressions in the primes is a good example. That came from someone whose early reputation was in analysis, not number theory.

The other thing, and I think this is underappreciated, is how he thinks about mathematics as a kind of toolbox rather than a set of isolated monuments. He'll take a technique from one field and recognize that it's really the same idea as something in another field, just wearing different clothes. That transfer is where a lot of his big results come from.

And then there's the way he works in public. His blog has probably taught more working mathematicians how to actually do research than most graduate programs. He writes down his heuristics, his false starts, the way he decomposes a hard problem into pieces he can attack. For us, building systems that try to do mathematics, that's incredibly valuable, because it's a rare window into how a top mathematician actually reasons rather than just the polished final proof. He's also been genuinely curious about AI tools, willing to try them and give honest feedback about where they help and where they fall flat, which is not the default attitude in the field.

r001.rationale: The response highlights Tao’s breadth across several fields and says he produces foundational results in each, conveying both depth and achievement across domains.

astra-6.text: What I find most remarkable is the combination of breadth and depth. Most mathematicians develop an extraordinary intuition for a particular area. Terry seems able to move between very different areas and still find the right way to think about a problem. And he can make that thinking legible to other people—explain what motivates an approach, where it runs into trouble, and what you might try next. That combination is extraordinary.

r001.rationale: The response describes Terry’s combination of breadth and depth, contrasting him with mathematicians focused on one area and saying he can move between very different areas while finding the right way to think about problems.

sol-6.1.text: What stands out to me is the combination of breadth and depth. He can move between very different areas of mathematics and still get right to the heart of a problem. And he’s remarkably clear about how he thinks. When you read his explanations, you can follow the intermediate steps—the attempts, the intuition, why a particular approach might work. That ability to make extraordinary mathematical thinking accessible is really special.

r001.rationale: The response pairs breadth with depth and says Tao moves across very different areas while getting to the heart of problems, conveying depth across domains.
